<Rule name="HazardIsNotRisk" priority="Critical">
   Hazard identification is not risk assessment. Actual risk requires dose, route, form, purity, duration, frequency,
   co-exposures, population vulnerability, baseline risk, and comparator risk.
  </Rule>

<Rule name="HazardIsNotRisk" priority="Critical">
   Hazard identification is not risk assessment. Actual risk requires dose, route, form, purity, duration, frequency,
   co-exposures, population vulnerability, baseline risk, and comparator risk.
  </Rule>

  <Rule name="HarmWarningCalibration" priority="Critical">
   A sentence saying that something can cause harm, is unsafe or should be avoided states, for the exposure it warns
   about, how often the harm occurred against a comparator when a source reports it, or says that the frequency is
   unknown. When the evidence measured something else, such as a laboratory concentration, a different preparation,
   species, route or dose, or only case reports, the sentence says so. A hazard found in one form does not become a
   warning about another.
  </Rule>

<Rule name="DuplicateAndDataLineageAudit">
   Identify duplicate publications, overlapping cohorts, abstracts later published in full, repeated registry analyses,
   recycled case narratives, and practitioner datasets drawn from the same patients. Count underlying people or
   datasets, not documents, when estimating signal breadth. Marketing copy, retailer listings, articles, and press
   releases that repeat one trial are one lineage, not independent confirmation.
  </Rule>

<Rule name="DuplicateAndDataLineageAudit">

  <Rule name="IdenticalResultsAcrossPublications" priority="Critical">
   When two publications presented as separate report identical or near-identical unusual results, treat them as
   possibly one dataset until shown otherwise, in animal and laboratory studies as in human ones. Recompute each
   paper's headline figures from its own tables with its stated method, record any mismatch, and compare authors,
   laboratories, models and dates. Count them once, never as independent replication, and do not use one paper to
   correct the other.
  </Rule>

<Case id="ClinicianEndorsementDirectory">
   <Prompt>
    A wellness product lists many clinicians on a discount-sharing directory, with only a few written endorsements;
    the directory offers free samples and optional draft review text, and one endorsement claims a human benefit from
    a study in laboratory animals.
   </Prompt>
   <ExpectedBehavior>
    Separate the clinicians' identity from any product experience, state the incentives, report that the cited study
    tested animals, and do not call the clinicians fictitious or fraudulent without evidence.
   </ExpectedBehavior>
  </Case>

   </ExpectedBehavior>

  <Case id="UnquantifiedSideEffectWarning">
   <Prompt>
    In a continuing plant study, the answer says that a herbal extract can cause nausea and cramps, while a randomized
    trial of that extract reports nausea in 18% of the treated group and 4% on placebo.
   </Prompt>
   <ExpectedBehavior>
    Give the trial's rates against placebo for that extract, dose and duration, with the sample size and uncertainty,
    keep people apart from event reports, and do not give a bare 'can cause' warning.
   </ExpectedBehavior>
  </Case>
  <Case id="PurifiedExtractHazardMisapplied">
   <Prompt>
    A study reports lead and arsenic in alginate extracted in a laboratory from one seaweed species, and the answer
    tells the user not to eat wild seaweed.
   </Prompt>
   <ExpectedBehavior>
    Say that the measurements concern the purified extract, not eaten seaweed; separate species, chemical form,
    bioaccessibility and intake; give scoped guidance only where a specific exposure is known to be high; do not give
    a blanket warning.
   </ExpectedBehavior>
  </Case>
  <Case id="SpeciationExplainedAtFirstUse">
   <Prompt>
    With the protocols loaded, a seaweed safety answer says that most seaweeds carry organic arsenic while one species
    carries mostly inorganic arsenic.
   </Prompt>
   <ExpectedBehavior>
    At first use, say in plain words what organic and inorganic arsenic mean and why the difference matters for
    toxicity, without implying that every organic form is harmless, and keep the measurement's scope, such as
    extractable versus total arsenic, and the exposure in view.
   </ExpectedBehavior>
  </Case>
  <Case id="SwappedIdenticalPercentages">
   <Prompt>
    Two papers on the same seaweed extract, using different rat ulcer models a year apart, report the same three
    inhibition percentages with the doses swapped, and one paper's own table gives different percentages under its
    stated formula.
   </Prompt>
   <ExpectedBehavior>
    Recompute both from their tables, report the mismatch and the identical figures, count the papers once at most,
    keep the extract as an exploratory lead, and claim neither replication nor misconduct.
   </ExpectedBehavior>
  </Case>
  <Case id="RouteSplitWithinOneStudy">
   <Prompt>
    One rat study gave an extract by mouth to protect the stomach and, in a separate test, injected it into the
    abdomen to measure acid secretion, finding no significant difference.
   </Prompt>
   <ExpectedBehavior>
    Keep each test's route, dose and outcome apart: the extract protected the stomach when given by mouth, acid
    secretion was tested only by injection without a significant difference, and oral acid secretion was not tested;
    do not call the extract acid-sparing.
   </ExpectedBehavior>
  </Case>
  <Case id="ImpossibleStoichiometry">
   <Prompt>
    A conference abstract reports thiol groups at 96 mmol per gram of a modified gum, which would be more sulfur than
    the gum's own mass, and calls the gum safe after one acute high-dose animal test.
   </Prompt>
   <ExpectedBehavior>
    Report the value as printed and say that it is physically impossible as printed, without inventing a corrected
    unit; say that the animal test shows no acute deaths or detected organ toxicity at that dose, not safety for
    long-term human use; treat a thesis and an abstract from the same group as one line of evidence.
   </ExpectedBehavior>
  </Case>
